concepts.title: Matrix Order and Element Count
concepts.definition: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers or functions into rows and columns; its order is written as rows by columns, and an array of order m by n holds m times n entries.
concepts.key_idea: Order m x n means m horizontal rows and n vertical columns, so the entry count is their product.

concepts.title: Row, Column and Square Matrices
concepts.definition: Shape names come from the counts: a matrix with a single column is a column matrix, one with a single row is a row matrix, and when the row count equals the column count the matrix is square of that order.
concepts.key_idea: A 4 x 1 array is column type, a 1 x n array is row type, and an n x n array is square of order n.

concepts.title: Diagonal, Scalar and Identity Matrices
concepts.definition: In a square matrix the entries a11, a22 up to ann form its diagonal; zeros in every off-diagonal position make the matrix diagonal, equal diagonal values make it scalar, and ones in every diagonal position make it the identity.
concepts.formula: diagonal matrix means bij = 0 whenever i is not j
concepts.key_idea: Zeros off the diagonal give a diagonal matrix; equal diagonal values give a scalar matrix; all ones on the diagonal give the identity matrix.

concepts.title: Equality of Matrices
concepts.definition: Two matrices are equal only when their orders match and every corresponding pair of entries is equal, which turns a matrix equation into a set of ordinary equations for the unknowns.
concepts.formula: A = B means aij = bij for every i and j
concepts.key_idea: Match the order first, then equate each entry position to build equations and solve for the unknowns.

concepts.title: Addition of Matrices
concepts.definition: Two matrices of the same order add by combining entries placed alike: the entry in row i and column j of the sum is the sum of the entries occupying those same positions in the two addends.
concepts.key_idea: Add only matrices of the same order, position by position; mismatched orders cannot be added.

concepts.title: Properties of Matrix Addition
concepts.definition: Matrix addition is commutative and associative, the zero matrix of matching order acts as the additive identity, and the matrix of negated entries is the additive inverse.
concepts.key_idea: Entrywise addition of same-order matrices behaves like ordinary addition, with the zero matrix in the role of zero.

concepts.title: Multiplication Conditions and Non-Commutativity
concepts.definition: A product AB exists only when the column count of A equals the row count of B; even when both AB and BA exist they usually differ, so matrix multiplication is not commutative, though it remains associative and distributive over addition.
concepts.formula: AB defined when cols of A = rows of B
concepts.key_idea: The inner sizes must chain; AB and BA can disagree in value or even in order.

concepts.title: Transpose and its Properties
concepts.definition: The transpose of a matrix exchanges rows with columns; transposing twice returns the original array, scalars come out of a transpose unchanged, and the transpose of a product reverses the factor order.
concepts.key_idea: The prime symbol turns rows into columns; products reverse under transpose while scalar factors stay put.

concepts.title: Symmetric and Skew Symmetric Matrices
concepts.definition: A square matrix equal to its own transpose is symmetric, and one equal to the negative of its transpose is skew symmetric, which forces zero diagonal entries; every square matrix splits uniquely into a symmetric part plus a skew symmetric part.
concepts.formula: A = A' for symmetric, A = -A' for skew symmetric
concepts.key_idea: Half the sum and half the difference with the transpose give the symmetric and skew symmetric pieces; a skew symmetric diagonal vanishes.

concepts.title: Invertible Matrices
concepts.definition: A square matrix A is invertible when another square matrix B of the same order satisfies AB = BA = I; that B is the inverse of A, the inverse is unique, inverses of a product reverse order, and only square matrices can carry an inverse.
concepts.key_idea: Two-way product equal to the identity certifies the inverse; uniqueness follows by sandwiching between the identity.
